Table of Contents 01 I. Background Overview 02 II. Solution 03 III. Detailed Module Design 04 IV. Effect Comparison 05 V. Summary 06 VI. Related Resources I. Background Overview As the OpenClaw ecosystem becomes increasingly rich, more and more developers configure a large number of Skills for their OpenClaw instances to expand capability boundaries. However, a problem that is easy to overlook emerges: when the number of skills grows from a single digit to dozens or even hundreds, each conversation injects all skill descriptions into the System Prompt, resulting in significant Token waste and rising costs. 1.1 OpenClaw's Skills Mechanism OpenClaw adopts the AgentSkills specification for its skill directory structure. Each skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file, which defines the name, description, and metadata via YAML frontmatter. OpenClaw loads skills from three locations; when a skill with the same name exists, it is overridden according to the following priority (from high to low): Workspace Skills: located in the skills/ directory under the workspace directory, with the highest priority Managed Skills: located in ~/.openclaw/skills/, shared across workspaces Bundled Skills: built in with the OpenClaw installation package When available skills exist, OpenClaw injects a compact XML list into the System Prompt: available_skills skill name feishu-doc /name description Feishu document read/write operations... /description location ~/.openclaw/extensions/feishu/skills/feishu-doc/SKILL.md /location /skill !-- more skills... -- /available_skills According to the official OpenClaw documentation, the Token overhead of this list is deterministic, and its calculation formula is: Total characters = 195 (base overhead) + for each Skill (97 + name length + description length + location length) [Figure 1] After the model identifies a relevant skill, it loads the full content of the corresponding SKILL.md on demand via the read tool to obtain detailed instructions. When the number of skills grows to 30, 50, or even more, the skill list itself generates considerable Token consumption. An intuitive example: when the user says "Help me check the Feishu document", the System Prompt injects descriptions of 50 skills such as weather query, music playback, email management, etc., of which only feishu-doc, feishu-wiki, and feishu-drive are related to the request. This means most of the skill description Tokens are wasted. II. Solution This article introduces an intelligent Skill recall solution for OpenClaw called ISS (Intelligent Skill Selection), based on Amazon Bedrock Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon S3 Vector, which uses vector semantic retrieval to achieve on-demand skill recall, reducing the Token of skill descriptions injected into each conversation by about 90%, and improving response speed. Among them: Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings: provides high-quality text vectorization capabilities, mapping skill descriptions and user queries into a 1024-dimensional vector space, supporting semantic-level similarity calculation. The latency for a single embedding generation is about 150ms, billed per call, with no need to maintain a separate embedding service. Amazon S3 Vector: serves as the persistent storage layer for vector data, eliminating the need to manage vector database instances or indexes; S3, as a fully managed object storage, automatically handles availability and durability. The vector for each skill is stored as a JSON file, containing skill metadata and a 1024-dimensional embedding vector.
